Hands-on Exercise 8: Market Area Analysis with the Huff Model

  • Show All Code
  • Hide All Code
  • View Source
Author

JUNCHEN LI

Published

October 22, 2026

Modified

October 22, 2026

Overview

How do distance and competition shape a store’s potential market area? This exercise follows Chapter 18 and applies the Huff model to the supplied Taichung teaching data. I prepare village population and store sales, construct an origin–destination distance matrix, map the patronage probability for store BT, and compare population-based allocations with recorded sales.

The model is an illustrative allocation among the supplied stores. It is not a calibrated forecast of current demand, revenue or profitability.

1 Data sources and acquisition

The chapter’s data section names the inputs but supplies no direct download link. Its local paths are not working public downloads. The data used here come from the user-downloaded course archive Hands-on_Ex08.zip, installed from the local Downloads folder. No inputs were downloaded from the instructor’s GitHub repository. The archive checksum and installation record are in data/source-manifest.txt.

Input Role Local location
STORES_TC and shapefile companions Locations and identifiers of the study stores data/geospatial/
TOWN_TC and shapefile companions District boundaries for map context data/geospatial/
VILLAGE_TC and shapefile companions Village polygons and join keys data/geospatial/
pop2019.csv December 2019 households and population data/aspatial/
Store_sales_data.csv Store-level bill and sales records requiring aggregation data/aspatial/

The chapter’s introductory list uses _TN, but its Taichung import code uses _TC and also reads TOWN_TC. This exercise follows those actual imports. The alternative STORES_TC1 layer is not substituted. GIS metadata files ending in .qmd are not Quarto documents and are excluded from the website source tree.

To reproduce the exercise, obtain the matching course package through the instructor’s authorised distribution channel, then place the files in the locations above. Do not replace the 2019 population with a recent release without reconciling geography and documenting the change. Keep raw files unchanged and check their redistribution permissions before publishing them.

Packages

The workflow uses the chapter’s sf, MCI, tmap and ggstatsplot tools, with explicit tidyverse components. Install missing packages before rendering; the document checks dependencies without installing software automatically.

Show code 
packages <- c("sf", "dplyr", "tidyr", "readr", "ggplot2", "MCI",
              "tmap", "ggstatsplot", "knitr")
missing_packages <- packages[!vapply(packages, requireNamespace,
                                    logical(1), quietly = TRUE)]
if (length(missing_packages)) {
  stop("Install these packages before rendering: ",
       paste(missing_packages, collapse = ", "))
}
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tmap)
library(knitr)
tmap_mode("plot")
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
fmt <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)

2 Importing and checking the inputs

Spatial layers and coordinate reference systems

The supplied layers describe TWD97 / TM2 zone 121. Read their stored CRS definitions and transform them to EPSG:3826, a projected CRS in metres. Assigning a CRS label would not transform coordinates. Geometry checks precede distance calculation.

Show code 
read_projected <- function(layer) {
  x <- st_read(paste0("data/geospatial/", layer, ".shp"), quiet = TRUE)
  if (is.na(st_crs(x))) stop("Missing CRS for ", layer)
  st_transform(x, 3826) |> st_make_valid()
}
stores <- read_projected("STORES_TC") |> arrange(Store_CD)
town <- read_projected("TOWN_TC")
village_raw <- read_projected("VILLAGE_TC") |> arrange(VILLCODE)
stopifnot(!anyNA(stores$Store_CD), !anyDuplicated(stores$Store_CD),
          !anyNA(village_raw$VILLCODE), !anyDuplicated(village_raw$VILLCODE),
          all(st_is_valid(village_raw)), !any(st_is_empty(village_raw)),
          !any(st_is_empty(stores)))
kable(data.frame(Layer = c("Stores", "Districts", "Villages"),
                 Features = c(nrow(stores), nrow(town), nrow(village_raw)),
                 EPSG = 3826))
Layer Features EPSG
Stores 28 3826
Districts 28 3826
Villages 622 3826
Show code 
tm_shape(village_raw) + tm_polygons(fill = "grey93", col = "grey75") +
  tm_shape(town) + tm_borders(col = "grey40") +
  tm_shape(stores) + tm_dots(fill = "#b2182b", col = "white", size = 0.9) +
  tm_title("Taichung teaching-data study area") +
  tm_scalebar() + tm_compass(type = "arrow")

These polygons define the supplied study extent, rather than a claim to cover every current administrative unit. The store set defines the competitors considered by the model; omitted stores and alternative brands are outside its choice set.

Population and sales tables

Read identifiers as text to preserve leading zeros and separators. Retain only the population columns needed for joining and interpretation; this avoids duplicated geographic-name columns.

Show code 
pop2019 <- read_csv("data/aspatial/pop2019.csv",
                   col_types = cols(V_ID = col_character()),
                   show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(V_ID = gsub("-", "", V_ID, fixed = TRUE))
store_sales <- read_csv("data/aspatial/Store_sales_data.csv",
                       col_types = cols(`Store Code` = col_character()),
                       show_col_types = FALSE)
stopifnot(!anyNA(pop2019$V_ID), !anyDuplicated(pop2019$V_ID))
kable(data.frame(Input = c("Population rows", "Sales rows"),
                 Records = c(nrow(pop2019), nrow(store_sales))))
Input Records
Population rows 625
Sales rows 5499

3 Data preparation

Aggregating and matching store sales

The sales table includes stores outside the spatial layer. Aggregate by store code, then match only the supplied study stores. Missing store identifiers and unmatched sales-store codes are counted, not treated as extra Taichung competitors. Sales amounts are not used as attractiveness, avoiding a circular comparison against the same sales observations later.

Show code 
sales_in_scope <- store_sales |>
  filter(`Store Code` %in% stores$Store_CD)
stopifnot(all(is.finite(sales_in_scope$Bills)),
          all(is.finite(sales_in_scope$Amount)),
          all(sales_in_scope$Bills >= 0), all(sales_in_scope$Amount >= 0))
store_sales_aggre <- sales_in_scope |>
  group_by(`Store Code`) |>
  summarise(Total_Bill = sum(Bills), Total_Sales = sum(Amount),
            .groups = "drop")
stores <- stores |>
  left_join(store_sales_aggre, by = c("Store_CD" = "Store Code"),
            relationship = "one-to-one") |>
  mutate(Store_size = 100)
stopifnot(!anyNA(stores$Total_Sales), !anyNA(stores$Total_Bill))
kable(data.frame(Check = c("Sales rows without a store code",
                           "Non-missing sales codes outside the study layer",
                           "Matched study stores", "Matched sales records"),
                 Count = c(sum(is.na(store_sales$`Store Code`)),
                           n_distinct(store_sales$`Store Code`[
                             !is.na(store_sales$`Store Code`) &
                             !store_sales$`Store Code` %in% stores$Store_CD]),
                           nrow(stores), nrow(sales_in_scope))))
Check Count
Sales rows without a store code 29
Non-missing sales codes outside the study layer 205
Matched study stores 28
Matched sales records 678

All stores receive the chapter’s illustrative attractiveness of 100. This is not measured floor area. Equal attractiveness makes baseline probabilities depend only on relative distance.

Joining population and documenting exclusions

Remove the hyphen from V_ID before matching it to VILLCODE. Use explicit join keys and a one-to-one relationship. An unmatched polygon is not assumed to contain zero people.

Show code 
population_fields <- pop2019 |>
  select(V_ID, H_CNT, P_CNT, M_CNT, F_CNT, INFO_TIME)
unmatched_population <- population_fields |>
  anti_join(st_drop_geometry(village_raw), by = c("V_ID" = "VILLCODE"))
village_joined <- village_raw |>
  left_join(population_fields, by = c("VILLCODE" = "V_ID"),
            relationship = "one-to-one")
excluded_villages <- village_joined |> filter(is.na(P_CNT))
village <- village_joined |> filter(!is.na(P_CNT))
stopifnot(nrow(village) > 0,
          all(is.finite(village$P_CNT)), all(village$P_CNT >= 0),
          !anyNA(st_drop_geometry(village)[c("H_CNT", "M_CNT", "F_CNT")]))
kable(data.frame(Check = c("Input village polygons", "Population-unmatched polygons",
                           "Retained villages", "Population rows without a polygon",
                           "Retained population", "Male/female reconciliation differences"),
                 Value = c(nrow(village_raw), nrow(excluded_villages),
                           nrow(village), nrow(unmatched_population), sum(village$P_CNT),
                           sum(village$M_CNT + village$F_CNT != village$P_CNT))),
      format.args = list(big.mark = ","))

The current files retain 617 villages and exclude 5 polygons without population. The exclusions follow the chapter but may leave geographic gaps. Population-table rows without matching polygons are outside this spatial allocation, and should not be silently redistributed.

4 Computing the distance and interaction matrices

Use st_point_on_surface() to obtain one point inside each village. Although the chapter describes these as centroids, the function returns an interior representative point. Distances are straight-line metres from these points to stores, not road-network distance or travel time. Large villages may be poorly represented by one point.

Show code 
village_center <- st_point_on_surface(village)
distmat <- st_distance(village_center, stores)
D <- matrix(as.numeric(distmat), nrow = nrow(village), ncol = nrow(stores),
            dimnames = list(village$VILLCODE, stores$Store_CD))
stopifnot(all(is.finite(D)), all(D > 0))
distmat_long <- as.data.frame(D) |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("VILLCODE") |>
  pivot_longer(-VILLCODE, names_to = "Store_CD", values_to = "distance")
interaction_matrix <- distmat_long |>
  left_join(st_drop_geometry(stores) |> select(Store_CD, Store_size),
            by = "Store_CD", relationship = "many-to-one") |>
  select(VILLCODE, Store_CD, Store_size, distance) |> as.data.frame()
stopifnot(nrow(interaction_matrix) == nrow(village) * nrow(stores),
          !anyDuplicated(interaction_matrix[c("VILLCODE", "Store_CD")]),
          !anyNA(interaction_matrix))
kable(data.frame(Pairs = nrow(interaction_matrix),
                 Minimum_m = min(D), Median_m = median(D), Maximum_m = max(D)),
      digits = 1)
Pairs Minimum_m Median_m Maximum_m
17276 108.5 11965.3 41395.4

Zero distances would make the inverse-power model undefined. The assertion stops rather than silently choosing an arbitrary offset. The full matrix includes every retained village–store pair, with IDs retained through all transformations.

5 Computing and validating Huff probabilities

For village \(i\) and store \(j\), the model is

\[p_{ij}=\frac{A_j^{\gamma}d_{ij}^{\lambda}}{\sum_k A_k^{\gamma}d_{ik}^{\lambda}}.\]

Follow the MCI defaults: \(\gamma=1\), \(\lambda=-2\), and power functions for attraction and distance. Negative \(\lambda\) reduces attraction with distance. The denominator normalises probabilities over the supplied stores, so each village’s probabilities must sum to one. There is no outside option for not purchasing or choosing an omitted competitor.

Show code 
huff_share <- MCI::huff.shares(interaction_matrix, "VILLCODE", "Store_CD",
                               "Store_size", "distance",
                               gamma = 1, lambda = -2,
                               atype = "pow", dtype = "pow")
huff_share <- as_tibble(huff_share) |>
  mutate(VILLCODE = as.character(VILLCODE), Store_CD = as.character(Store_CD))
probability_checks <- huff_share |>
  group_by(VILLCODE) |> summarise(probability_sum = sum(p_ij), .groups = "drop")
manual <- interaction_matrix |>
  group_by(VILLCODE) |>
  mutate(manual_p = Store_size * distance^(-2),
         manual_p = manual_p / sum(manual_p)) |> ungroup()
comparison <- huff_share |>
  left_join(manual |> select(VILLCODE, Store_CD, manual_p),
            by = c("VILLCODE", "Store_CD"), relationship = "one-to-one")
stopifnot(nrow(huff_share) == nrow(interaction_matrix),
          all(is.finite(huff_share$p_ij)), all(huff_share$p_ij >= 0),
          all(huff_share$p_ij <= 1),
          max(abs(probability_checks$probability_sum - 1)) < 1e-10,
          max(abs(comparison$p_ij - comparison$manual_p)) < 1e-10)
kable(data.frame(Check = c("Largest origin-sum error", "Largest formula-check error"),
                 Error = c(max(abs(probability_checks$probability_sum - 1)),
                           max(abs(comparison$p_ij - comparison$manual_p)))), digits = 12)
Check Error
Largest origin-sum error 0
Largest formula-check error 0

The independent formula check tests numerical agreement with MCI, not real-world validity. Multiplying every distance by the same unit-conversion factor leaves these power-model probabilities unchanged because that common factor cancels. Equal attractiveness similarly cancels from each origin’s probability ratios.

6 Trade-area analysis for store BT

The chapter’s narrative mentions TG once, but its selection and map use BT. Use BT consistently. Join its probability by village code, and keep missing-population polygons in grey for context.

Show code 
market_share <- huff_share |> filter(Store_CD == "BT")
selected_store <- stores |> filter(Store_CD == "BT")
stopifnot(nrow(selected_store) == 1, nrow(market_share) == nrow(village))
trade_area <- village |>
  left_join(market_share |> select(VILLCODE, p_ij), by = "VILLCODE",
            relationship = "one-to-one")
Show code 
tm_shape(village_raw) + tm_polygons(fill = "grey90", col = "white") +
  tm_shape(trade_area) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "p_ij",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 10,
                                               values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "BT probability")) +
  tm_shape(town) + tm_borders(col = "grey40", lwd = 0.5) +
  tm_shape(selected_store) + tm_dots(fill = "red", col = "black", size = 1.3) +
  tm_title("Potential market area of store BT") +
  tm_compass(type = "arrow") + tm_scalebar()

The highest village-level BT probability is 0.944. Quantile classes distribute villages across colour groups, rather than defining equal probability intervals or an observed catchment boundary. Darker areas indicate stronger relative attraction under the assumed parameters, not demonstrated customer loyalty.

7 Allocating population and comparing recorded sales

Append population to each village–store probability and use shares.total() to compute \(E_j=\sum_i P_i p_{ij}\). Since the input market size is a population count, \(E_j\) is a population allocation, not dollars or recorded customers. Revenue estimation would additionally require a compatible spending rate, time period and calibrated purchase behaviour. The chapter’s sales comparison is retained as an exploratory association.

Show code 
huff_share_pp <- huff_share |>
  left_join(st_drop_geometry(village) |> select(VILLCODE, P_CNT),
            by = "VILLCODE", relationship = "many-to-one") |> as.data.frame()
huff_total <- MCI::shares.total(huff_share_pp, "VILLCODE", "Store_CD",
                                "p_ij", "P_CNT")
huff_total$suppliers_single <- as.character(huff_total$suppliers_single)
store_sales_est <- stores |>
  left_join(huff_total, by = c("Store_CD" = "suppliers_single"),
            relationship = "one-to-one")
store_sales_nongeom <- st_drop_geometry(store_sales_est)
stopifnot(!anyNA(store_sales_est$sum_E_j),
          abs(sum(store_sales_est$sum_E_j) - sum(village$P_CNT)) < 1e-6)
allocation_check <- huff_share_pp |>
  group_by(Store_CD) |> summarise(manual_total = sum(P_CNT * p_ij), .groups = "drop")
allocation_check <- left_join(allocation_check, store_sales_nongeom,
                              by = "Store_CD", relationship = "one-to-one")
stopifnot(max(abs(allocation_check$manual_total - allocation_check$sum_E_j)) < 1e-6)
kable(store_sales_nongeom |> arrange(desc(sum_E_j)) |>
        select(Store_CD, sum_E_j, Total_Bill, Total_Sales), digits = 1,
      col.names = c("Store", "Allocated population", "Recorded bills", "Recorded sales"))

Stores Pearson_r Spearman_rho
28 0.576 0.573

The observed Pearson correlation is 0.576 and Spearman’s rank correlation is 0.573. These describe this store sample; they do not establish causal effects or out-of-sample forecast accuracy. Allocations share a common population total and competing choice set, so independent-store inference is questionable. The supplied sales period and currency are not independently documented here, and population refers to December 2019.

8 Probability table and distance-decay sensitivity

Wide probability matrix

Following the chapter’s final step, retain one row per village and one column per store. The preview shows only a few columns for readability; the exported table contains all stores.

Show code

  pivot_wider(names_from = Store_CD, values_from = p_ij)
stopifnot(nrow(huff_share_wider) == nrow(village),
          ncol(huff_share_wider) == nrow(stores) + 1)

Supplement: alternative distance exponents

Compare \(\lambda=-1,-2,-3\) while keeping the origins, competitors and equal attractiveness fixed. This supplements the chapter and does not fit parameters to sales. Stronger distance decay concentrates probabilities on nearer stores. With equal attractiveness, the most probable store is the nearest one regardless of these negative exponents; uncertainty and total allocations can still change substantially.

Show code 
scenarios <- lapply(c(-1, -2, -3), function(exponent) {
  result <- MCI::huff.shares(interaction_matrix, "VILLCODE", "Store_CD", "Store_size",
                             "distance", gamma = 1, lambda = exponent)
  as_tibble(result) |>
    mutate(VILLCODE = as.character(VILLCODE), Store_CD = as.character(Store_CD),
           lambda = exponent)
}) |> bind_rows()
scenario_origins <- scenarios |>
  group_by(lambda, VILLCODE) |>
  summarise(probability_sum = sum(p_ij), maximum_probability = max(p_ij),
            .groups = "drop")
stopifnot(max(abs(scenario_origins$probability_sum - 1)) < 1e-10)
scenario_totals <- scenarios |>
  left_join(st_drop_geometry(village) |> select(VILLCODE, P_CNT),
            by = "VILLCODE", relationship = "many-to-one") |>
  group_by(lambda, Store_CD) |>
  summarise(allocated_population = sum(P_CNT * p_ij), .groups = "drop")
scenario_summary <- scenario_origins |>
  group_by(lambda) |>
  summarise(mean_maximum_probability = mean(maximum_probability), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(scenario_totals |> filter(Store_CD == "BT") |>
              select(lambda, BT_allocated_population = allocated_population), by = "lambda")
kable(scenario_summary, digits = 3,
      col.names = c("Distance exponent", "Mean maximum probability", "BT population allocation"))
Distance exponent Mean maximum probability BT population allocation
-3 0.654 137499.7
-2 0.475 138306.0
-1 0.204 128640.1
Show code 
ggplot(scenario_totals, aes(Store_CD, allocated_population,
                            colour = factor(lambda), group = factor(lambda))) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Store code", y = "Allocated population", colour = "Distance exponent") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

This comparison reveals parameter dependence, not which exponent is correct. Empirical customer-origin data would be needed for defensible calibration and an independent validation design.

9 Findings, limitations and reproducibility

The model allocates 2,804,359 residents across 28 stores using 17,276 origin–destination pairs. Store BT receives 138,306 population-equivalents under the baseline. These totals reconcile with retained population, but they are conditional model outputs rather than observed patronage.

The main limitations are uniform store attractiveness, straight-line distance, one representative point per village, missing population matches, historical population, an incomplete choice set and an undocumented sales period. No parameter was selected to maximise a reported association. Customer surveys, measured floor area, compatible expenditure data and network travel costs would be needed before making investment recommendations.

# Overview

How do distance and competition shape a store's potential market area? This exercise follows [Chapter 18](https://r4gdsa.netlify.app/chap18) and applies the Huff model to the supplied Taichung teaching data. I prepare village population and store sales, construct an origin–destination distance matrix, map the patronage probability for store BT, and compare population-based allocations with recorded sales.

The model is an illustrative allocation among the supplied stores. It is not a calibrated forecast of current demand, revenue or profitability.

# 1 Data sources and acquisition

The chapter's [data section](https://r4gdsa.netlify.app/chap18#the-data) names the inputs but supplies no direct download link. Its local paths are not working public downloads. The data used here come from the user-downloaded course archive **Hands-on_Ex08.zip**, installed from the local Downloads folder. No inputs were downloaded from the instructor's GitHub repository. The archive checksum and installation record are in `data/source-manifest.txt`.

| Input | Role | Local location |
|---|---|---|
| `STORES_TC` and shapefile companions | Locations and identifiers of the study stores | `data/geospatial/` |
| `TOWN_TC` and shapefile companions | District boundaries for map context | `data/geospatial/` |
| `VILLAGE_TC` and shapefile companions | Village polygons and join keys | `data/geospatial/` |
| `pop2019.csv` | December 2019 households and population | `data/aspatial/` |
| `Store_sales_data.csv` | Store-level bill and sales records requiring aggregation | `data/aspatial/` |

The chapter's introductory list uses `_TN`, but its Taichung import code uses `_TC` and also reads `TOWN_TC`. This exercise follows those actual imports. The alternative `STORES_TC1` layer is not substituted. GIS metadata files ending in `.qmd` are not Quarto documents and are excluded from the website source tree.

To reproduce the exercise, obtain the matching course package through the instructor's authorised distribution channel, then place the files in the locations above. Do not replace the 2019 population with a recent release without reconciling geography and documenting the change. Keep raw files unchanged and check their redistribution permissions before publishing them.

## Packages

The workflow uses the chapter's `sf`, `MCI`, `tmap` and `ggstatsplot` tools, with explicit tidyverse components. Install missing packages before rendering; the document checks dependencies without installing software automatically.

```{r}
#| label: setup
packages <- c("sf", "dplyr", "tidyr", "readr", "ggplot2", "MCI",
              "tmap", "ggstatsplot", "knitr")
missing_packages <- packages[!vapply(packages, requireNamespace,
                                    logical(1), quietly = TRUE)]
if (length(missing_packages)) {
  stop("Install these packages before rendering: ",
       paste(missing_packages, collapse = ", "))
}
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tmap)
library(knitr)
tmap_mode("plot")
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
fmt <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
```

# 2 Importing and checking the inputs

## Spatial layers and coordinate reference systems

The supplied layers describe TWD97 / TM2 zone 121. Read their stored CRS definitions and transform them to EPSG:3826, a projected CRS in metres. Assigning a CRS label would not transform coordinates. Geometry checks precede distance calculation.

```{r}
#| label: spatial-import
read_projected <- function(layer) {
  x <- st_read(paste0("data/geospatial/", layer, ".shp"), quiet = TRUE)
  if (is.na(st_crs(x))) stop("Missing CRS for ", layer)
  st_transform(x, 3826) |> st_make_valid()
}
stores <- read_projected("STORES_TC") |> arrange(Store_CD)
town <- read_projected("TOWN_TC")
village_raw <- read_projected("VILLAGE_TC") |> arrange(VILLCODE)
stopifnot(!anyNA(stores$Store_CD), !anyDuplicated(stores$Store_CD),
          !anyNA(village_raw$VILLCODE), !anyDuplicated(village_raw$VILLCODE),
          all(st_is_valid(village_raw)), !any(st_is_empty(village_raw)),
          !any(st_is_empty(stores)))
kable(data.frame(Layer = c("Stores", "Districts", "Villages"),
                 Features = c(nrow(stores), nrow(town), nrow(village_raw)),
                 EPSG = 3826))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-study-area
#| fig-cap: "Supplied study villages, district boundaries and store locations."
tm_shape(village_raw) + tm_polygons(fill = "grey93", col = "grey75") +
  tm_shape(town) + tm_borders(col = "grey40") +
  tm_shape(stores) + tm_dots(fill = "#b2182b", col = "white", size = 0.9) +
  tm_title("Taichung teaching-data study area") +
  tm_scalebar() + tm_compass(type = "arrow")
```

These polygons define the supplied study extent, rather than a claim to cover every current administrative unit. The store set defines the competitors considered by the model; omitted stores and alternative brands are outside its choice set.

## Population and sales tables

Read identifiers as text to preserve leading zeros and separators. Retain only the population columns needed for joining and interpretation; this avoids duplicated geographic-name columns.

```{r}
#| label: tabular-import
pop2019 <- read_csv("data/aspatial/pop2019.csv",
                   col_types = cols(V_ID = col_character()),
                   show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(V_ID = gsub("-", "", V_ID, fixed = TRUE))
store_sales <- read_csv("data/aspatial/Store_sales_data.csv",
                       col_types = cols(`Store Code` = col_character()),
                       show_col_types = FALSE)
stopifnot(!anyNA(pop2019$V_ID), !anyDuplicated(pop2019$V_ID))
kable(data.frame(Input = c("Population rows", "Sales rows"),
                 Records = c(nrow(pop2019), nrow(store_sales))))
```

# 3 Data preparation

## Aggregating and matching store sales

The sales table includes stores outside the spatial layer. Aggregate by store code, then match only the supplied study stores. Missing store identifiers and unmatched sales-store codes are counted, not treated as extra Taichung competitors. Sales amounts are not used as attractiveness, avoiding a circular comparison against the same sales observations later.

```{r}
#| label: sales-join
sales_in_scope <- store_sales |>
  filter(`Store Code` %in% stores$Store_CD)
stopifnot(all(is.finite(sales_in_scope$Bills)),
          all(is.finite(sales_in_scope$Amount)),
          all(sales_in_scope$Bills >= 0), all(sales_in_scope$Amount >= 0))
store_sales_aggre <- sales_in_scope |>
  group_by(`Store Code`) |>
  summarise(Total_Bill = sum(Bills), Total_Sales = sum(Amount),
            .groups = "drop")
stores <- stores |>
  left_join(store_sales_aggre, by = c("Store_CD" = "Store Code"),
            relationship = "one-to-one") |>
  mutate(Store_size = 100)
stopifnot(!anyNA(stores$Total_Sales), !anyNA(stores$Total_Bill))
kable(data.frame(Check = c("Sales rows without a store code",
                           "Non-missing sales codes outside the study layer",
                           "Matched study stores", "Matched sales records"),
                 Count = c(sum(is.na(store_sales$`Store Code`)),
                           n_distinct(store_sales$`Store Code`[
                             !is.na(store_sales$`Store Code`) &
                             !store_sales$`Store Code` %in% stores$Store_CD]),
                           nrow(stores), nrow(sales_in_scope))))
```

All stores receive the chapter's illustrative attractiveness of 100. This is not measured floor area. Equal attractiveness makes baseline probabilities depend only on relative distance.

## Joining population and documenting exclusions

Remove the hyphen from `V_ID` before matching it to `VILLCODE`. Use explicit join keys and a one-to-one relationship. An unmatched polygon is not assumed to contain zero people.

```{r}
#| label: population-join
population_fields <- pop2019 |>
  select(V_ID, H_CNT, P_CNT, M_CNT, F_CNT, INFO_TIME)
unmatched_population <- population_fields |>
  anti_join(st_drop_geometry(village_raw), by = c("V_ID" = "VILLCODE"))
village_joined <- village_raw |>
  left_join(population_fields, by = c("VILLCODE" = "V_ID"),
            relationship = "one-to-one")
excluded_villages <- village_joined |> filter(is.na(P_CNT))
village <- village_joined |> filter(!is.na(P_CNT))
stopifnot(nrow(village) > 0,
          all(is.finite(village$P_CNT)), all(village$P_CNT >= 0),
          !anyNA(st_drop_geometry(village)[c("H_CNT", "M_CNT", "F_CNT")]))
kable(data.frame(Check = c("Input village polygons", "Population-unmatched polygons",
                           "Retained villages", "Population rows without a polygon",
                           "Retained population", "Male/female reconciliation differences"),
                 Value = c(nrow(village_raw), nrow(excluded_villages),
                           nrow(village), nrow(unmatched_population), sum(village$P_CNT),
                           sum(village$M_CNT + village$F_CNT != village$P_CNT))),
      format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
kable(st_drop_geometry(excluded_villages) |> select(VILLCODE, VILLENG),
      col.names = c("Excluded village code", "Village label"))
```

The current files retain **`r nrow(village)` villages** and exclude **`r nrow(excluded_villages)`** polygons without population. The exclusions follow the chapter but may leave geographic gaps. Population-table rows without matching polygons are outside this spatial allocation, and should not be silently redistributed.

# 4 Computing the distance and interaction matrices

Use `st_point_on_surface()` to obtain one point inside each village. Although the chapter describes these as centroids, the function returns an interior representative point. Distances are straight-line metres from these points to stores, not road-network distance or travel time. Large villages may be poorly represented by one point.

```{r}
#| label: distances
village_center <- st_point_on_surface(village)
distmat <- st_distance(village_center, stores)
D <- matrix(as.numeric(distmat), nrow = nrow(village), ncol = nrow(stores),
            dimnames = list(village$VILLCODE, stores$Store_CD))
stopifnot(all(is.finite(D)), all(D > 0))
distmat_long <- as.data.frame(D) |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("VILLCODE") |>
  pivot_longer(-VILLCODE, names_to = "Store_CD", values_to = "distance")
interaction_matrix <- distmat_long |>
  left_join(st_drop_geometry(stores) |> select(Store_CD, Store_size),
            by = "Store_CD", relationship = "many-to-one") |>
  select(VILLCODE, Store_CD, Store_size, distance) |> as.data.frame()
stopifnot(nrow(interaction_matrix) == nrow(village) * nrow(stores),
          !anyDuplicated(interaction_matrix[c("VILLCODE", "Store_CD")]),
          !anyNA(interaction_matrix))
kable(data.frame(Pairs = nrow(interaction_matrix),
                 Minimum_m = min(D), Median_m = median(D), Maximum_m = max(D)),
      digits = 1)
```

Zero distances would make the inverse-power model undefined. The assertion stops rather than silently choosing an arbitrary offset. The full matrix includes every retained village–store pair, with IDs retained through all transformations.

# 5 Computing and validating Huff probabilities

For village $i$ and store $j$, the model is

$$p_{ij}=\frac{A_j^{\gamma}d_{ij}^{\lambda}}{\sum_k A_k^{\gamma}d_{ik}^{\lambda}}.$$

Follow the [MCI defaults](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/MCI/refman/MCI.html): $\gamma=1$, $\lambda=-2$, and power functions for attraction and distance. Negative $\lambda$ reduces attraction with distance. The denominator normalises probabilities over the supplied stores, so each village's probabilities must sum to one. There is no outside option for not purchasing or choosing an omitted competitor.

```{r}
#| label: huff-baseline
huff_share <- MCI::huff.shares(interaction_matrix, "VILLCODE", "Store_CD",
                               "Store_size", "distance",
                               gamma = 1, lambda = -2,
                               atype = "pow", dtype = "pow")
huff_share <- as_tibble(huff_share) |>
  mutate(VILLCODE = as.character(VILLCODE), Store_CD = as.character(Store_CD))
probability_checks <- huff_share |>
  group_by(VILLCODE) |> summarise(probability_sum = sum(p_ij), .groups = "drop")
manual <- interaction_matrix |>
  group_by(VILLCODE) |>
  mutate(manual_p = Store_size * distance^(-2),
         manual_p = manual_p / sum(manual_p)) |> ungroup()
comparison <- huff_share |>
  left_join(manual |> select(VILLCODE, Store_CD, manual_p),
            by = c("VILLCODE", "Store_CD"), relationship = "one-to-one")
stopifnot(nrow(huff_share) == nrow(interaction_matrix),
          all(is.finite(huff_share$p_ij)), all(huff_share$p_ij >= 0),
          all(huff_share$p_ij <= 1),
          max(abs(probability_checks$probability_sum - 1)) < 1e-10,
          max(abs(comparison$p_ij - comparison$manual_p)) < 1e-10)
kable(data.frame(Check = c("Largest origin-sum error", "Largest formula-check error"),
                 Error = c(max(abs(probability_checks$probability_sum - 1)),
                           max(abs(comparison$p_ij - comparison$manual_p)))), digits = 12)
```

The independent formula check tests numerical agreement with MCI, not real-world validity. Multiplying every distance by the same unit-conversion factor leaves these power-model probabilities unchanged because that common factor cancels. Equal attractiveness similarly cancels from each origin's probability ratios.

# 6 Trade-area analysis for store BT

The chapter's narrative mentions TG once, but its selection and map use **BT**. Use BT consistently. Join its probability by village code, and keep missing-population polygons in grey for context.

```{r}
#| label: bt-selection
market_share <- huff_share |> filter(Store_CD == "BT")
selected_store <- stores |> filter(Store_CD == "BT")
stopifnot(nrow(selected_store) == 1, nrow(market_share) == nrow(village))
trade_area <- village |>
  left_join(market_share |> select(VILLCODE, p_ij), by = "VILLCODE",
            relationship = "one-to-one")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-bt-probability
#| fig-cap: "Modelled patronage probability for BT, conditional on the supplied store choice set. Grey background includes villages excluded for missing population."
tm_shape(village_raw) + tm_polygons(fill = "grey90", col = "white") +
  tm_shape(trade_area) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "p_ij",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 10,
                                               values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "BT probability")) +
  tm_shape(town) + tm_borders(col = "grey40", lwd = 0.5) +
  tm_shape(selected_store) + tm_dots(fill = "red", col = "black", size = 1.3) +
  tm_title("Potential market area of store BT") +
  tm_compass(type = "arrow") + tm_scalebar()
```

The highest village-level BT probability is **`r sprintf('%.3f', max(trade_area$p_ij))`**. Quantile classes distribute villages across colour groups, rather than defining equal probability intervals or an observed catchment boundary. Darker areas indicate stronger relative attraction under the assumed parameters, not demonstrated customer loyalty.

# 7 Allocating population and comparing recorded sales

Append population to each village–store probability and use `shares.total()` to compute $E_j=\sum_i P_i p_{ij}$. Since the input market size is a population count, $E_j$ is a **population allocation**, not dollars or recorded customers. Revenue estimation would additionally require a compatible spending rate, time period and calibrated purchase behaviour. The chapter's sales comparison is retained as an exploratory association.

```{r}
#| label: population-allocation
huff_share_pp <- huff_share |>
  left_join(st_drop_geometry(village) |> select(VILLCODE, P_CNT),
            by = "VILLCODE", relationship = "many-to-one") |> as.data.frame()
huff_total <- MCI::shares.total(huff_share_pp, "VILLCODE", "Store_CD",
                                "p_ij", "P_CNT")
huff_total$suppliers_single <- as.character(huff_total$suppliers_single)
store_sales_est <- stores |>
  left_join(huff_total, by = c("Store_CD" = "suppliers_single"),
            relationship = "one-to-one")
store_sales_nongeom <- st_drop_geometry(store_sales_est)
stopifnot(!anyNA(store_sales_est$sum_E_j),
          abs(sum(store_sales_est$sum_E_j) - sum(village$P_CNT)) < 1e-6)
allocation_check <- huff_share_pp |>
  group_by(Store_CD) |> summarise(manual_total = sum(P_CNT * p_ij), .groups = "drop")
allocation_check <- left_join(allocation_check, store_sales_nongeom,
                              by = "Store_CD", relationship = "one-to-one")
stopifnot(max(abs(allocation_check$manual_total - allocation_check$sum_E_j)) < 1e-6)
kable(store_sales_nongeom |> arrange(desc(sum_E_j)) |>
        select(Store_CD, sum_E_j, Total_Bill, Total_Sales), digits = 1,
      col.names = c("Store", "Allocated population", "Recorded bills", "Recorded sales"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-sales-comparison
#| fig-cap: "Exploratory association across study stores. The axes have different units; this is not a predicted-versus-observed revenue calibration plot."
ggstatsplot::ggscatterstats(
  data = store_sales_nongeom, x = sum_E_j, y = Total_Sales,
  type = "parametric", marginal = FALSE,
  xlab = "Huff-allocated population", ylab = "Recorded sales amount (source units)",
  title = "Population allocation and recorded store sales")
```

```{r}
#| label: association-summary
pearson_r <- cor(store_sales_nongeom$sum_E_j, store_sales_nongeom$Total_Sales)
spearman_r <- cor(store_sales_nongeom$sum_E_j, store_sales_nongeom$Total_Sales,
                  method = "spearman")
kable(data.frame(Stores = nrow(stores), Pearson_r = pearson_r,
                 Spearman_rho = spearman_r), digits = 3)
```

The observed Pearson correlation is **`r sprintf('%.3f', pearson_r)`** and Spearman's rank correlation is **`r sprintf('%.3f', spearman_r)`**. These describe this store sample; they do not establish causal effects or out-of-sample forecast accuracy. Allocations share a common population total and competing choice set, so independent-store inference is questionable. The supplied sales period and currency are not independently documented here, and population refers to December 2019.

# 8 Probability table and distance-decay sensitivity

## Wide probability matrix

Following the chapter's final step, retain one row per village and one column per store. The preview shows only a few columns for readability; the exported table contains all stores.

```{r}
#| label: wide-probabilities
huff_share_wider <- huff_share |> select(VILLCODE, Store_CD, p_ij) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Store_CD, values_from = p_ij)
stopifnot(nrow(huff_share_wider) == nrow(village),
          ncol(huff_share_wider) == nrow(stores) + 1)
kable(head(huff_share_wider[, seq_len(min(6, ncol(huff_share_wider)))], 6), digits = 4)
```

## Supplement: alternative distance exponents

Compare $\lambda=-1,-2,-3$ while keeping the origins, competitors and equal attractiveness fixed. This supplements the chapter and does not fit parameters to sales. Stronger distance decay concentrates probabilities on nearer stores. With equal attractiveness, the most probable store is the nearest one regardless of these negative exponents; uncertainty and total allocations can still change substantially.

```{r}
#| label: sensitivity
scenarios <- lapply(c(-1, -2, -3), function(exponent) {
  result <- MCI::huff.shares(interaction_matrix, "VILLCODE", "Store_CD", "Store_size",
                             "distance", gamma = 1, lambda = exponent)
  as_tibble(result) |>
    mutate(VILLCODE = as.character(VILLCODE), Store_CD = as.character(Store_CD),
           lambda = exponent)
}) |> bind_rows()
scenario_origins <- scenarios |>
  group_by(lambda, VILLCODE) |>
  summarise(probability_sum = sum(p_ij), maximum_probability = max(p_ij),
            .groups = "drop")
stopifnot(max(abs(scenario_origins$probability_sum - 1)) < 1e-10)
scenario_totals <- scenarios |>
  left_join(st_drop_geometry(village) |> select(VILLCODE, P_CNT),
            by = "VILLCODE", relationship = "many-to-one") |>
  group_by(lambda, Store_CD) |>
  summarise(allocated_population = sum(P_CNT * p_ij), .groups = "drop")
scenario_summary <- scenario_origins |>
  group_by(lambda) |>
  summarise(mean_maximum_probability = mean(maximum_probability), .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(scenario_totals |> filter(Store_CD == "BT") |>
              select(lambda, BT_allocated_population = allocated_population), by = "lambda")
kable(scenario_summary, digits = 3,
      col.names = c("Distance exponent", "Mean maximum probability", "BT population allocation"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-sensitivity
#| fig-cap: "Store population allocations under three uncalibrated distance-decay assumptions."
ggplot(scenario_totals, aes(Store_CD, allocated_population,
                            colour = factor(lambda), group = factor(lambda))) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Store code", y = "Allocated population", colour = "Distance exponent") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

This comparison reveals parameter dependence, not which exponent is correct. Empirical customer-origin data would be needed for defensible calibration and an independent validation design.

# 9 Findings, limitations and reproducibility

The model allocates **`r fmt(sum(village$P_CNT))` residents** across **`r nrow(stores)` stores** using **`r fmt(nrow(interaction_matrix))` origin–destination pairs**. Store BT receives **`r fmt(round(store_sales_est$sum_E_j[store_sales_est$Store_CD == 'BT']))` population-equivalents** under the baseline. These totals reconcile with retained population, but they are conditional model outputs rather than observed patronage.

The main limitations are uniform store attractiveness, straight-line distance, one representative point per village, missing population matches, historical population, an incomplete choice set and an undocumented sales period. No parameter was selected to maximise a reported association. Customer surveys, measured floor area, compatible expenditure data and network travel costs would be needed before making investment recommendations.

```{r}
write_csv(huff_share_wider, "outputs/village_store_probabilities.csv")
write_csv(store_sales_nongeom |> select(Store_CD, sum_E_j, Total_Bill, Total_Sales),
          "outputs/store_population_allocation.csv")
write_csv(scenario_totals, "outputs/distance_decay_sensitivity.csv")
raw_files <- list.files("data", recursive = TRUE, full.names = TRUE,
                        pattern = "\\.(csv|shp|shx|dbf|prj|cpg)$")
fingerprints <- data.frame(file = raw_files, md5 = unname(tools::md5sum(raw_files)))
write_csv(fingerprints, "outputs/input_fingerprints.csv")
```
